_readme: Model v4 — occupational fit before transferable-skill fit. This is an OVERLAY ON THE v3 OVERLAY, which is itself an overlay on config/profile.json: v4 keeps every axis, signal, combination and band v3 defined and adds the step the v3 board was missing. v3 asked 'how much of this posting's vocabulary is her vocabulary?' and answered honestly — which is how a Commercial/Transactional Lawyer reached 73 and a Child Psychologist 68, on 'review', 'accuracy', 'verification' and 'attention to detail'. Those words are transferable skills and they belong to every profession that writes things down. v4 asks the prior question first: is this an occupation she could plausibly hold? Only then does it score the four axes.
_occupationGateComment: STEP 1 — THE OCCUPATIONAL FIT GATE. Every posting is classified before scoring: CORE (the occupation itself is proofreading / copyediting / editorial or content quality / digital, marketing, email or creative QA), ADJACENT (a title she would not have searched for, whose primary responsibilities are still reviewing, editing, validating or quality-checking customer-facing, marketing, e-commerce or editorial content), or WRONG (a different profession whose description happens to contain her vocabulary). WRONG postings are suppressed. The class is a prerequisite and a multiplier, not another small signal: no quantity of transferable phrases moves a posting out of the class its occupation puts it in.

occupationGate._multipliersComment: Applied to the finished four-axis score. CORE is untouched; ADJACENT pays a small tariff for the uncertainty of an unfamiliar title; UNCLEAR — nothing in the posting says what the occupation is, usually a two-line snippet — is discounted and held below the apply bands; WRONG is discounted to nothing and suppressed by the pipeline.
occupationGate._capsComment: The hard ceiling per class, applied after the multiplier. The specification's floor requirement: a WRONG-occupation posting must never appear as a Strong or Good match on the strength of transferable skills, whatever else it scores. 34 sits far below every band and below the publish threshold, so these do not reach the board at all. UNCLEAR is capped at 69, which is one point under the 'possible adjacent opportunity' band: a posting that has not said what the job is cannot claim to be a good match. Note what changed when the threshold moved to 65 — an UNCLEAR posting can now be published, in the `low` band, where before the cap kept it off the board entirely. It is labelled Low priority and SKIP, which is the honest description of a posting whose occupation could not be read.
occupationGate._adjacentEvidenceComment: What an unfamiliar title has to show to count as ADJACENT rather than UNCLEAR. Core work signals are the evidence that the job is reviewing somebody else's work against a standard (proofreading, final review, accuracy, standards, audit); contentDomain is the evidence that the thing being reviewed is content rather than payroll, casework or code. Both are required — that pairing is the whole gate. A combination hit, which is v3's strongest evidence, substitutes for the second core signal.
occupationGate._contentDomainComment: The subject matter that makes reviewing work HER kind of reviewing work. Deliberately about the thing being reviewed — copy, campaigns, product pages, course materials — and never about the act of reviewing, which the core signals already cover.
occupationGate._coreFamilyTiersComment: Which of v3's role-family tiers count as CORE occupations on their own. A title in one of these families states the occupation, so it needs no further proof — 'Copy Editor' is a copy editor. v3's `adjacent` tier (quality-review-adjacent: QA Specialist, Quality Analyst and the rest) deliberately does NOT appear here: those titles are held by software testers, manufacturing inspectors and clinical auditors as often as by content people, so they must earn their class from the description like any other unfamiliar title.
occupationGate._wrongOccupationsComment: STEP 1(C) — the professions whose vocabulary overlaps hers and whose work does not. Each entry is recognised two ways. A `titles` hit is conclusive: the employer has named the occupation in the job title and no description can argue with it. A `body` hit needs `bodyThreshold` DISTINCT concepts, because one stray 'patient' or 'litigation' in a company blurb is not a profession — this is the specification's STEP 5 rule that a posting is not rejected because the word 'health' or 'legal' appears somewhere. `weakTitles` are titles that point at the occupation without settling it — Program Coordinator, Case Manager, Technician are held by content people too — so they classify only when the description corroborates them with at least one occupation concept. `credentials` are the STEP 2 eligibility gate and are listed with the occupation they belong to, because a credential is only disqualifying when it is the credential for the job being advertised.

wrongOccupations.label: Legal practice
wrongOccupations.why: This is a lawyer's job. The reviewing in it is contract review, which is legal advice — the accuracy, verification and discrepancy language it shares with your work is the part of a lawyer's day that any careful professional would recognise, not an opening into the profession.

wrongOccupations.label: Clinical, medical or psychological practice
wrongOccupations.why: This is clinical practice. Assessment, evaluation and review here mean assessing people, and the profession is gated behind a licence.

wrongOccupations.label: Social work and child welfare
wrongOccupations.why: This is human-services casework. The compliance monitoring, quality improvement and documentation review in it are about the care of children and families, and the profession expects a social-work background.

wrongOccupations.label: Software, systems or hardware engineering
wrongOccupations.why: This is an engineering job. The verification and validation language in it is engineering verification — building and testing systems, not reading copy — and you have said plainly you do not want to move into development.

wrongOccupations.label: Software QA and test automation
wrongOccupations.why: This is software testing. It shares the letters QA with your job and almost nothing else: the object under test is an application, and the tools are test frameworks and code.
body: bug tracking in jira for builds

wrongOccupations.label: Accounting, audit and financial specialism
wrongOccupations.why: This is accounting. Reconciliation, audit and discrepancy work here means money, ledgers and controls, and the profession is built on a qualification you do not hold.

wrongOccupations.label: Scientific and regulatory specialism
wrongOccupations.why: This is scientific or regulatory work. The review in it is review of research or of a submission to a regulator, and it is gated behind a subject-matter doctorate or years in the field.

wrongOccupations.label: Sales, recruiting and account management
wrongOccupations.why: This is a quota-carrying or hiring job. The accuracy and detail language in it is about quotes, records and pipelines.

wrongOccupations.label: Trades, logistics and physical operations
wrongOccupations.why: This is hands-on operational work. Inspection and quality control here mean inspecting goods, vehicles or premises.

occupationGate._titleExemptionsComment: Occupation titles that are conclusive above cannot be read out of context: 'Content Engineer', 'Editorial Program Coordinator' and 'Documentation Specialist' contain an occupation word inside a content title. When one of these phrases is in the title, the title-level wrong-occupation test is skipped and the posting has to be classified on its description like any other — which is what should happen, because these titles genuinely go both ways.

_credentialGateComment: STEP 2 — the eligibility gate, kept separate from the occupation classes because a credential can appear in a posting whose occupation reads perfectly well. A hit here rejects the posting outright. The list is deliberately short and specific: it names credentials and professional backgrounds she demonstrably does not have and cannot acquire in the time it takes to apply. Everything softer — AP style, Chicago, a CMS, a PIM, an agency background, a proofreading tool — is a LEARNABLE GAP, lives in v3's qualification.learnableGaps, costs a few points and never blocks anything.

phrases.label: Scientific doctorate or regulated specialism
phrases: advanced degree in a scientific discipline

_orientationComment: STEP 4 — reviewing versus creating, with the specification's additions for v4: strategy ownership, demand generation and campaign strategy now count on the creation side, because a posting whose job is to OWN a marketing programme is not a posting whose job is to check one. 'Strategist' joins the creation titles for the same reason — a Senior Integrated Marketing Strategist is an adjacent industry and a poor functional fit, and it is the title that says so. The tariffs are unchanged from v3: writing being present is still not disqualifying, and a proofreading role that mentions writing clear feedback is still untouched.
_orientationAdditionsComment: Merged onto v3's lists rather than replacing them, so the shared vocabulary stays in one place. `creationTitlesAdded` are titles that state a creation or ownership job; `creationPhrasesAdded` are the responsibilities that mean the same thing.
_searchComment: STEP 8 — precision over volume, with the line drawn where v3 draws it. This started at 70, the specification's own 'possible adjacent opportunity' cutoff, and the first live run published six postings out of 995 — the occupational gate had already suppressed 225, and 378 more fell in the 65-69 band just underneath. Held at 65 the board keeps those, labelled honestly: 65-69 is the `low` band, so they print as Low priority and SKIP rather than being dressed up as opportunities. That is the trade this knob makes. Precision still comes from the occupational gate, which suppresses the wrong professions outright before this threshold is ever consulted; the threshold only decides how far down the plausible ones the list runs.
_surpriseComment: The Surprise Me shelf: one to three postings whose title is nothing she would have searched for and whose work is unusually well aligned anyway. This is how a Digital Content Integrity Coordinator gets found. Candidates must be ADJACENT — a core-family title is not a surprise, it is the search working — and must clear a high work-fit bar, because a surprise that turns out to be a mediocre match teaches her to stop reading the shelf.
_learnedPreferenceComment: STEP 7 — the explicit preferences, stated here so the board can protect them from inference. The 👍 / 👎 / 🚫 model may never learn a negative weight on any of these: several rejected postings happening to be full-time says nothing about full-time work, and a board that concluded otherwise would quietly delete a category she asked for.
